newsitem.title: FRANCE: French elections - how they vote.
newsitem.headline: French elections - how they vote.

text.p: Some 1,183 candidates will contest runoffs in 565 of France's 577 National Assembly constituencies in the decisive second round of a parliamentary election on Sunday, according to the Interior Ministry.
Only 12 deputies polled the 50 percent of the vote required to win a seat on the May 25 first round.
On Sunday, the candidate who wins the most votes in each single-member constituency is elected, even if he or she scores less than 50 percent.

There are 79 triangular contests, most involving a candidate from the extreme-right National Front. The rest are duels. Most are between the ruling centre-right coalition and a Socialist or Communist opposition candidate, although the National Front is on the ballot in 133 constituencies.
Any candidate who polled 12.5 percent of the number of registered voters was entitled to contest the second ballot.
President Jacques Chirac dissolved the lower house of parliament on April 21 and called a snap two-round election, 10 months ahead of schedule.
Article 12 of the 1958 constitution gives the president the right to dissolve the Assembly after consultations with the prime minister and the speakers of both houses of parliament.
A general election must be held 20 to 40 days after a decree is published in the Official Journal dissolving the Assembly.
The president, who appoints the prime minister and cabinet, may not dissolve parliament again in the first year of a new legislature.
The upper house, the Senate, is elected indirectly by local officials and is not affected by a dissolution of the Assembly.
There are 555 constituencies in metropolitan France and 22 in overseas departments and territories.
Voting takes place on Sunday from 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) to 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) in most areas and 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) in Paris and major provincial cities.

No results, projections or exit polls may be published until the last polling stations have closed in metropolitan France. By law, no opinion polls may be published in the last week before the first round or between the two rounds.
On election night, television stations broadcast generally reliable projections of the outcome in votes and seats as soon as the last polls close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).
Campaign spending and individual donations to parties are limited by law. The parties also receive public funds proportionate to the number of votes they poll.
The last parliamentary election took place in March 1993.
The state of the parties in the outgoing Assembly was:
RPR-UDF centre-right coalition 464
Socialist party and allies 61
Communist party and allies 24
Other left 14
Other right 13
Vacant seat 1
